#2020. Bayern won’t sign Rio Ngumoha after missing their chance in the summer – opinion

Bayern Munich are reportedly confident that there is a deal to be done with Liverpool for talented youngster Rio Ngumoha.

The Reds were understood to be the subject of some probing from the Bavarian giants, with discussions said to have taken place with the winger’s brother.

Whether Liverpool feel the same way… well, let’s just be clear on this: they don’t.

As Mick Brown noted in his latest report with Football Insider: “From what I hear, Bayern Munich are pretty confident there is a deal to be done.

“When there’s all this talk about making contact with his agents, speaking to the player, what it might cost, that stuff doesn’t happen unless they think they can do a deal.

“Whether Liverpool feel the same way, I have my doubts, because he has such obvious potential and Andoni Iraola has been pretty clear he is part of his plans.

“I don’t think he’s the finished article, but not many players are at 18, there are still areas of his game where he has to improve, so maybe that’s where the speculation comes from.”

Mick goes on to note that the Reds are currently giving Ngumoha everything he could realistically hope for at an elite European outfit. There is a pathway to the senior team and he’s already picked up 642 minutes (Transfermarkt) of action in the famous red shirt this season.

On top of that, his all-round game is being carefully developed, with appearances roughly split between both flanks.

And most importantly? Liverpool aren’t burning the player out — Andoni Iraola is managing the teenager’s minutes, rotating alongside Bradley Barcola, Victor Munoz and Cody Gakpo.

So, Bayern may feel a deal can be done, but realistically, can they offer the 18-year-old substantially more than he’s already receiving at Liverpool?

It’s worth pointing out that, as is indeed the case across Europe’s biggest outfits, Bayern’s shortlist is far from limited to Liverpool’s No.73. Names like Antonio Nusa and Oskar Pietuszewski are also highly rated by the club, with the former thought to be well-admired by Bayern chief Max Eberl.

But the important distinction to make here is that Ngumoha will not come cheap – far from it, compared to the two names alone we’ve just listed. And if Bayern already valued the versatile winger at €70m [£58.3m] in the summer, can you imagine how much his value has skyrocketed since becoming an important part of Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool squad? We’re surely talking in the territory of at least upwards of £7om, at a conservative estimate.

On that basis, options like Pietuszewski – who reportedly has a €60m [£50.1m] release clause at FC Porto – surely start to look more feasible for a club like Bayern that doesn’t necessarily have the same level of cash to splash as its Premier League counterparts.

#2018. Jack Grealish is EXILED by Everton: Ex-England star is still being left out, confirms boss David Moyes, after boozy nights at pubs and karaoke

By HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER

Published: 08:52 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 19:01 EST, 5 November 2026

David Moyes has confirmed that Jack Grealish will be absent for Everton's clash with Coventry City on Friday following disciplinary action last week - and said he may not even return after the international break.

The 31-year-old was dropped for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and will not be part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin tomorrow night.

'No, Jack is not available,' Moyes said on Thursday. 'I wouldn't give you the plan, but we will be working with Jack again soon.'

Moyes was then questioned by reporters whether the club and Grealish will mend their relationship over the upcoming international break, which is set to span two weeks.

'We'll see,' Moyes replied. 'We need to wait and see how things go.'

Asked if Grealish is currently training Moyes added: ‘I would rather not answer your question.’

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since rejoining Everton for a second season-long loan spell in the summer, has been exiled since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

The Manchester City loanee has since returned to training but is yet to feature for the club since the punishment, having missed both the Carabao Cup 3-1 win over Newcastle and the Premier League victory over the Magpies on Monday.

Jack Grealish remains exiled by Everton - with the winger not available for their game on Friday

Grealish has missed Everton's passed two games after being disciplined for missing training

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

It is thought Moyes had reservations about re-signing Grealish this summer after similar issues last season and last week the manager made it clear that he backed the 'club decision' to discipline the once England international.

Moyes said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision. It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Grealish is reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London. According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Their only injury concern ahead of the fixture is Jarrad Branthwaite, who Moyes admitted they have been nursing since he hobbled off late on at St. James' Park with cramp.

The Scot was speaking ahead of his 592nd game in charge of Everton, which will see him draw level with Harry Catterick’s record of the most games managed for the club.

‘I got told about it a few weeks ago,’ said Moyes, who has overseen more than 1,200 games during his coaching career. ‘I didn’t realise I’d got that close.

‘Harry Catterick’s name has always been mentioned alongside Howard [Kendall’s] name. I’m very proud to be up there, to be spoken of in terms of games. I wish I had the trophies to go with what they had.’

Victory over Coventry could see Everton move into the top-four places ahead of the November international break.

‘I think there’s lots to be positive about because of how they [the players] have been doing generally,’ said Moyes. ‘I feel we could have been doing better had we not lost some players last summer. I think it would have kept us right in and amongst it.

‘I think all you can try to do is get as many wins as you can and perform as well as we have. I think the players, in the main, have had good moments in games.’

Key to Everton’s form has been the goals of Thierno Barry. The 24-year-old has netted eight this term, already as many as he managed in his first season at the club.

Asked about the striker’s improvement, Moyes said: ‘I think the first thing is, he is settling down. We took a bit of an early gamble on buying Thierno and maybe knew he wouldn’t be right, right away. That’s been the case.

‘[Erling] Haaland should be worried that he’s just behind him now,’ he joked. ‘He has to be careful, Thierno is on his back.

‘Let’s hope he can keep scoring for us. He keeps trying to improve and I hope he can do that.’

#2012. Celtic come out swinging over Ross Desmond as Resolution 18 sparks defiant response

Celtic have come out swinging in defence of Ross Desmond and flatly refused demands for an apology over his explosive address at last year’s ill-fated AGM.

The Parkhead board have issued a stinging response to Resolution 18, which demands a “full and unreserved apology” to shareholders and supporters over the decision to allow Desmond to address the meeting despite holding no official role within Celtic PLC.

But Celtic have rejected the resolution “in its entirety” and accused those behind it of presenting a “misleading and inaccurate account” of what unfolded.

Desmond attended the explosive gathering as a representative of his father and Celtic's principal shareholder Dermot Desmond.

Read more: James Penrice reveals he considered quitting football before Rangers dream came true

His pre-written statement took aim at the club's detractors and accused some anti-board protestors of behaving like “bullies” as tensions inside the room boiled over.

The astonishing intervention was met with a furious reaction before the AGM descended into chaos and then-chairman Peter Lawwell eventually called time on proceedings.

But Celtic are having none of the suggestion that Desmond should never have been handed the floor.

The club insist he was perfectly entitled to address shareholders on his father's behalf and have described his speech as a “robust defence of Celtic Football Club, its long-term stewardship and the dedication of those responsible for its management.”

They also categorically reject allegations that Desmond and Lawwell conspired to orchestrate the premature ending of the meeting.

And when it comes to calls for an apology, Celtic's message ahead of the December 1 AGM could hardly be clearer.

Resolution 18 - The Chairman of the Board of Directors of Celtic PLC to Issue a full and unreserved apology to the shareholders and supporters of Celtic FC for giving a platform at the 2025 AGM to an individual who holds no role within the governance of Celtic PLC.

The Board rejects both the premise of this resolution and the misleading and inaccurate account of events presented in its supporting statement.

Ross Desmond attended the 2025 AGM as the representative of the Company’s largest shareholder, Dermot Desmond, as he has done on numerous previous occasions. His entitlement to attend and address the meeting was entirely legitimate and consistent with established corporate practice. The suggestion that his participation constituted an abuse of the AGM is without merit.

Equally, the allegation that Ross Desmond delivered an indiscriminate attack on Celtic supporters and shareholders is a gross misrepresentation of his remarks. His speech was a robust defence of Celtic Football Club, its long-term stewardship and the dedication of those responsible for its management.

It acknowledged mistakes and the need for continued improvement, while expressly praising the overwhelming majority of Celtic supporters for their passion, loyalty and commitment.

His criticism was directed at the conduct of a small minority whose behaviour, including personal abuse, intimidation and the deliberate fostering of hostility and division, he considered damaging to the Club. To characterise that criticism as an attack on Celtic supporters generally is demonstrably false.

The Board also categorically rejects the entirely baseless and serious insinuation that Ross Desmond and the then Chairman conspired to orchestrate the premature closure of the AGM. No such arrangement existed. Indeed, the meeting had already been disrupted and adjourned before Ross Desmond addressed shareholders.

The AGM was ultimately brought to a conclusion because further disruption made its orderly continuation impossible.

The Board fully respects the right of shareholders and supporters to express criticism and challenge the Club’s leadership, however robustly. But the right to express disagreement does not confer the right to intimidate others, prevent them from being heard or obstruct the proper conduct of a shareholders’ meeting.

The Board regrets that shareholders were denied the opportunity to participate fully in the Q&A due to the disruption caused at the 2025 AGM.

However, the Board will not apologise for permitting a duly authorised representative of a shareholder to address the meeting, nor will it accept the false characterisation of his remarks or the circumstances surrounding the meeting’s conclusion.

The Board rejects this resolution in its entirety and strongly recommends that shareholders vote against it.

#2010. Ruben Amorim rips into his AC Milan players after embarrassing Europa League defeat: Ex-Man United boss hits out at team's attitude and criticises 'awful' performance

Published: 16:34 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 5 November 2026

Ruben Amorim savaged his AC Milan side for their 'awful' attitude and performance in losing to Hungarian minnows Ferencvaros.

The former Man United boss presided over a 2-0 defeat in the Europa League on Thursday night in front of furious home supporters at the San Siro.

To make matters worse, the visitors even played the last 15 minutes with ten men but Milan were still unable to break through.

Amorim, 41, who was sacked from his post at Old Trafford last season and took over the Italian club in the summer, gave a brutal assessment of his team after the loss.

'When you play for Milan, you have a responsibility; you can't go out there like this,' he said at his post-match press conference.

'We're not ready to compete on both fronts in Serie A and Europe; we need to work on our approach to matches.

Ruben Amorim could hardly believe what he was seeing on a dreadful night for AC Milan

The home side suffered an embarrassing defeat by Ferencvaros at the San Siro

'There's nothing I can say tonight; we had to win; it was an important match. I can't say anything to defend the team; we need to understand what happened.'

He went on: 'Maybe I did something wrong in the last few days. Last year, the team had similar problems, and today we weren't ready; we didn't have the attitude to try to come back at all costs when we were behind.

'Tonight, we have no excuses. Whoever was on the pitch could have won this match. We have to resolve these ups and downs; we should have done many things much better, even just on second balls: that alone would have made things go differently.

'The first half, in particular, was awful; it's about ambition, attitude, and concentration. We weren't ready to move from the derby to another competition.'

Amorim's side are fifth in Serie A, seven points off top spot, and struggling massively in Europe down in 28th place – outside of the qualification spots for the knockout stages.

Even though Amorim made changes to the side that beat Inter in the derby at the weekend, he insisted the team should have had enough to beat Ferencvaros.

He went on: 'We're not mentally ready. The technical aspect has nothing to do with it. The rotation has nothing to do with it. You can't tell me that the starting line-up wasn't up to the task of winning the game.

'We gave ourselves all the chances we had, especially at the start. I take full responsibility for this, because the team is my responsibility, but we can't afford to do something like this, especially in the first half, in front of our fans, at our home. We can't do this; we have to improve, otherwise it's over.

'We want to do well in the Europa League too, we need to rotate and win like that too. We're not ready to play every three days now, but I certainly won't give up on the Europa League. We'll fight until it's over. It's a promise.'

Ferencvaros fans in the away end enjoyed one of the most memorable nights in their history

Amorim's results at AC Milan have been mixed after a positive start at his new club. He opted to take charge of the Italian giants having been out of work since his dismissal at United.

The Portuguese's reign at Old Trafford was disastrous. He oversaw the club's lowest Premier League finish (15th) after joining in November 2024.

And he only managed to win 38 per cent of United's games, taking 58 points from 47 games in the Premier League in total.

Amorim will hope the Ferencvaros result is a blip and AC Milan will have the chance to bounce back against Genoa on Sunday.

#2006. CM: Amorim let down again in another European debacle – the players whose stock has dropped

There are several players that are at risk of slipping down Ruben Amorim’s pecking order with displays like the one against Ferencvaros.

Calciomercato.com write that three clues add up to mean that we can say with certainty that Milan are not aiming to win the Europa League despite being one of the favourites, at least on paper. The defeats against Benfica, Bournemouth and Ferencvaros were determined by two factors.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The first is the attitude of the squad’s key players and the inadequacy of several reserves. The dominant Adrien Rabiot, for example, seems to sink when the Europa League anthem is played. The Frenchman – captain on this occasion due to Mike Maignan’s suspension – wasn’t the only culprit, but was certainly the most obvious.

The thing squad assembled last summer by Gerry Cardinale, Amorim and the management features a strong starting eleven that can compete with anyone (as was the case in the derby), but at the same time lacks alternatives.

In several cases, it’s fair to say that the players aren’t up to the task. Filippo Terracciano’s role is emblematic: already rejected by the previous management, he remained with Milan at Amorim’s request.

His season included 45 poorly played minutes against Benfica before being substituted at half-time, a straight red card as a substitute against Salzburg, and a poor performance against Ferencvaros that drew boos from the crowd.

Doubts are also growing over Ardon Jashari, who – after a few performances that were at least adequate – continues to display obvious technical and tactical limitations. The money spent on him (over €30m) is leading many to run out of patience.

The excellent performances against RB Salzburg and Udinese seemed to have reintroduced a courageous and powerful version of Davide Bartesaghi to Milan, but the most recent test saw him revert to the flaws of last season in terms of personality and concentration.

Pervis Estupinan, on the other hand, seems to have completely disappeared from the radar, having remained on the bench for the entire match against Ferencvaros. The two left-backs have a lot of work to do, and this could influence some transfer choices too.

The answer ultimately depends on the system. If we’re using 3-4-2-1, I’d put him in as the right-sided AM, with Puli on the left. My ideal formation is 4-3-3, in which case I’d put him in as the RW. I guess then I’d still use him as the RW in a 4-2-3-1.

RB/RWB, again depends on what we’re talking about. We have two injuries in that position, so do we need one in the short term? Maybe yes, but I’m talking long term. Given that we’ll get Athekame back in the summer, I don’t think we need another one. Athekame will start, Saelemaekers can back him up.

Re backup striker, I think you’re right. We might need one in January.

Two injuries but neither of them is a right back, Chukwueze shouldn’t be used as a RWB while Alexis is an ideal profile for that. Moreira is a versatile player but still a LWB by nature, after all, that is what he has been playing most of the time so far.

If he had been a coach that I rated and wanted brought to the club, I would 100% be a lot more patient. Heck, I wanted Farioli the summer they appointed Allegri. But since I think Amorim was also another “panic buy”, my personal leash is going to be very short. Remember how they interviewed 2-3 coaches before him? Iraola was the no. 1 target…

He proved that a long time ago. You just didn’t want to accept Tare did a bad job and signed a total loser.

#2005. SPFL record transfer tipped, Rangers bluff called, Celtic blockbuster predicted

Welcome to The Burning Questions, our daily debate where we take one major subject in Scottish sport and tackle the three questions everyone is talking about.

This time, the January transfer window is under the spotlight, with Celtic and Rangers facing some potentially huge decisions.

Matt O’Riley’s £30million move remains the Scottish transfer record, but could a pair of stars be poised to smash it?

Then there’s January itself. Both have emerged as prized assets for their clubs, but could either be at risk of a big-money move when the window opens?

And finally, what blockbuster business could be on the cards? From record sales to shock signings, there could yet be some major movement on both sides of Glasgow.

Jonny McFarlane and Graeme Young give their answers to today’s three Burning Questions.

The £30m Celtic received for Matt O’Riley remains the Scottish transfer record. Will it survive the next two windows, and who is the player most likely to smash it?

Jonny McFarlane: It's a toss-up between Camilo Duran and Olwethu Makhanya. Both have been outstanding this season and should smash that glass ceiling. The Rangers man is hampered by the lack of European football, and English scouts in particular might struggle to raise too much enthusiasm for performances against what they see as 'Scottish dross'. That might allow Derek McInnes to hold on to his star for another season, but when the time is right, the club will surely scoop a record fee for a defender who has everything in his locker to be a success in the modern game.

Duran is more likely to go sooner. He's already got a superb Champions League record from his time at Qarabag and has continued that form, despite his team's struggles, at home and on the continent. His stay in Scotland will be short and the fee a record departure for a player who has a higher level in his game than Scottish football.

Graeme Young: I have been so impressed with Makhanya, but goals are what make the world go round in our beautiful game. Duran is a stick-on to go for big money. Scouts in England were well aware of the Colombia international before he signed for Celtic, and he brings a double whammy when it comes to his potential fee when it's time to depart.

His analytics are off the charts and he passes the eye test by making the difference in the biggest games. Duran can play multiple positions and appeals to clubs across Europe due to his versatility and knack for making the difference. Teams will likely curse themselves for not beating Celtic to the punch. However, they also won't baulk at paying at least four times what Celtic did when they forked out £6m to lure him from Azerbaijan.

Is there a fear both Olwethu Makhanya and Camilo Duran could be prime targets for other clubs in January? If so, are either, or both, at risk of being sold?

Jonny McFarlane: The Scottish game saw a £40m cash injection evaporate overnight when both Rangers and Celtic saw Youssef Chermiti and Alistair Johnston's potential transfers wiped out by injury. That outcome won't be forgotten by either club.

Rangers in particular will be stung by the big striker's injury, given the likelihood of cashing in for a record fee on their young striker, who had finally come good towards the end of the season. The Govan club also have recent, painful history of not taking big offers for star players and losing them down the line for nothing. If Rangers are to start matching Celtic as a selling club and make their player-trading model work, they need to start selling players. Losing anyone in the midst of a title race isn't ideal, but money talks.

With tens of millions in the bank, Martin O'Neill is under no pressure to sell anyone, but I'd be surprised if Duran isn't a player in a hurry. At 25 in February, he's got a short window where he's at an attractive age, something that won't be lost on his advisors, who will be seeing pound signs.

Graeme Young: Jonny nails it with that key point regarding both teams being burned in the summer. However, there's every chance both of these teams will be locked in a title battle which could go the distance. Makhanya looks one of the best finds in recent memory, with Duran not far behind.

Those two are almost certain to see out the season, but don't rule out a raft of loan-to-buy or temporary exits when the January sales start. Bojan Miovski is a prime candidate to explore opportunities elsewhere if Lawrence Shankland returns at full capacity.

And what about Sebastian Tounekti? The Tunisia international is cast in the wrong movie, and he's likely fourth choice on the left behind Yang, Jota and Callum Osmand. I know English Championship sides mulled a late move for him in the days before he left Hammarby for Celtic. That could be an option once again.

And finally, no sitting on the fence: give us one bold prediction for the January transfer window. A blockbuster sale, shock signing, record fee or something completely out of left field.

Jonny McFarlane: Celtic are always a hard club to predict. You'd have to imagine they will look to add starting quality to this flawed squad, but January is always difficult for that. A midfielder with legs to replace Engels will surely arrive.

At Ibrox, the one to watch out for is Manny Fernandez. He's had poor moments, but he's a data standout and any top-five league club looking for a central defender who's good in the air will have him near the top of their list of options. Make no mistake, clubs in big leagues are watching him.

I wouldn't be at all surprised if he ends up in the Premier League, where he also qualifies as homegrown despite his status as a Nigeria international. Will that be January? It's not what Rangers would ideally want, but a fee north of £15m would surely be enough.

Graeme Young: This is an easy one for me. Andrew Cavenagh is setting everyone up for a blockbuster January window. The American intimated it would be quiet for the Ibrox side, but I'm not buying it. The man who once revealed he had a live transfer data screen close by during signing season isn't likely to sit back and refuse to roll the dice if the title and, whisper it, a potential Treble are up for grabs.

Across the city, the transfer talk is rightfully centred around a long-running hunt for a proper defensive midfielder. However, I believe the most expensive signing of the window could be a big-money central defender.

#2004. 'Severe rowdy' behaviour fears over changes to York City's home ground

Proposals for the LNER Community Stadium include a self-service ‘Box Bar’ to cut queues, reducing its licensed hours, indoor sports matches broadcasts and outdoor events and performances.

An application from the stadium’s operator stated the Box Bar would improve customer service by increasing the points of sale for alcohol which would cut queues at peak times.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

But two objectors who have bought homes in the nearby Castra Park development said they feared the changes would threaten the peace and quiet of the family neighbourhood.

York Council environmental health officer Michael Golightly said the application should be refused on public nuisance grounds as the potential effects of the changes could not be measured.

It comes as Greenwich Leisure Ltd’s (GLL) application is set to go before councillors for a decision on Monday, November 16.

Changes proposed for the stadium, at Huntington’s Monks Cross Shopping Park, include allowing outdoor events including boxing and wrestling matches, live music and other performances.

Plans to host six events a year including three boxing and wrestling matches within the stadium bowl in May and June have been drawn up.

Those plans, lodged by the York Stadium Management Company, are being dealt with under a separate application.

The stadium’s licensed hours would also be reduced from the current 2am to 11.30pm daily.

Sales would still be permitted from 8am across all of the 8,500-capacity stadium’s licensed areas.

Non-sporting events such as showing televised matches on screens would also be permitted.

The venue would also be licensed to hold indoor sporting events and other performances, stage live music and play recorded music.

The stadium would be operational from 6am to midnight every day.

Plans stated the self-service Box Bar will be supervised by at least two members of staff to intervene if issues arise and prevent service to under 18s.

They added the stadium’s licensed areas would be monitored by CCTV at all times and other measures would be in place to manage licensed activities.

The measures, including plans to manage events where 500 or more people are set to attend, have been agreed by operator GLL and North Yorkshire Police.

But a resident who is set to move into Castra Park, which is on land between the stadium complex and Huntington’s New Lane, said they were extremely concerned.

The objector said: “Introducing a fast-service Box Bar designed to increase the speed and volume of alcohol sales, combined with broadcasting non-sporting televised events, will generate a severe public nuisance.

“The resulting noise, shouting, and rowdy crowd dispersal at 11:30pm will cut directly into the peace and quiet of a brand-new residential family neighbourhood.”

Another future Castra Park resident said the roughly 300 new homes at the development would be exposed to late-night noise if the plans go ahead.

They said: “Increasing alcohol availability and extending operational hours will draw larger, less predictable crowds into an area that now borders new residential streets and pedestrian routes.

“This raises legitimate concerns about antisocial behaviour, crowd management, and the safety of residents who will be living within metres of the stadium perimeter.”

Published: 18:32 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 19:13 EST, 5 November 2026

England have privately asked Chelsea for the latest on Cole Palmer ahead of Thomas Tuchel revealing his squad for the Nations League clashes with Croatia and Spain.

Palmer is under consideration for another call-up, having withdrawn from duty during the last international break with a minor muscular injury.

Tuchel responded by appearing to question his desire to represent his country, warning he 'misses way too many camps' as the 24-year-old skipped all four England fixtures in September and October.

Palmer had played a full 90 for Chelsea away at Bournemouth before that break, which he then used to fly abroad to the Caribbean with his girlfriend, Olivia Holder, after withdrawing from England duty. He was accompanied by a personal rehab coach on that trip, and was provided with an injury-specific training and recovery plan by his club.

Palmer started in Chelsea's first fixture when the Premier League returned at home to Brentford with Blues boss Xabi Alonso insisting they were right to take care of their star player themselves.

Chelsea star Cole Palmer is under consideration for England UEFA Nations League call-up

Palmer, who was injured, went to the Caribbean with girlfriend Olivia Holder on the last international break

It has been described as standard procedure for England to make medical checks on players with clubs. While it does not guarantee a call-up, it indicates how Tuchel has been weighing up offering Palmer another chance as he names his next squad on Friday morning.

Palmer was not the only player to withdraw from England duty in the last break, with Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento among other dropouts.

During the last international break, during which the Three Lions completed four fixtures, Pickford and Trafford played in two each.

Tuchel said: “Traff gets regular starts now, that’s what we wanted. James Trafford did well. They shared the matches last time. I’m not sure what we will do. There’s an opportunity that we maybe do this again.

“I have to speak with our goalkeeper coach. But the goalkeepers, they are a bit of a unit for themselves, and rightly so.

Trafford made a £40m switch from Manchester City to Leeds in the summer and is benefiting from regular football.

He played second-fiddle to Gianluigi Donnarumma across the Pennines, yet now sits comfortably at the top of the pecking order in West Yorkshire.

Alongside Pickford and Trafford in the Three Lions squad is Brighton & Hove Albion’s Jason Steele, who is uncapped and appears unlikely to see any action.

#1998. John McGlynn backed for Aberdeen leap as Craig Levein questions lack of recognition

With John McGlynn being suggested as an option for the Aberdeen job, Craig Levein feels the Falkirk manager deserves the chance to take charge of a club of that ilk. In fact, he cannot believe it has not happened already.

Following Stephen Robinson’s sacking on Monday, the Pittodrie hotseat is vacant and given McGlynn’s body of work at his current club, he is likely to be at least mentioned when club chiefs gather to compile a list of candidates.

After taking over when Falkirk were in League One, leading them to an unbeaten season, back-to-back promotions and a top-six finish that looks like being repeated, he is a manager who should be on the radar of many clubs.

Levein, who worked with the 64-year-old at Hearts, is perplexed as to why that does not appear to have been the case.

Asked if he is surprised McGlynn has not had a job of that size already, he responded: “That’s the question. His body of work in the last seven or eight years is exceptional.

“Obviously, he was at Hearts. Then he went to Raith Rovers and Falkirk. Falkirk were really struggling when he went in there and what he’s managed to do is remarkable. He’s dragged them into the Premiership, and if you look at them, they’ve been fantastic.

“He’s a really good manager. He’s meticulous when it comes to his detail. I don’t think Falkirk will thank me for saying this, but I think he deserves an opportunity to go to a bigger club and see if he can do the same thing again.”

McGlynn is a totally different manager to the one who took charge of the Tynecastle club 14 years ago, having been influenced by Brendan Rodgers during a stint scouting for him at Celtic.

A more attractive, pleasing-on-the-eye style of football has earned his Falkirk side rave reviews. It has not gone unnoticed how hard his team works at the same time, a product of the old school streak that still exists within him.

“He plays a style of football which I think probably relates back to his time at Celtic under Brendan Rodgers. If you watched John’s teams before and after that, there was a massive change in how he played.

“He’s developed that and he’s got Falkirk on everybody’s lips just now. Nobody wants to play them because they’re playing so well.

“He’s taken some players who have not really been that successful elsewhere and turned them into guys who can play top-flight football and look like they were born to do it.

“He’s a very thoughtful guy. If you look at what he’s done, you have to ask why he isn’t getting the recognition he probably deserves.

“I have a bias because I like the guy and I want to see him do really well, but I think he deserves it,” said Levein.

Why North Macedonia star is confident they can stun Scotland at Hampden Key Switzerland star ruled out of Scotland Nations Leage clash with injury

The former Scotland manager will be watching as Sebastien Pocognoli’s team take on North Macedonia and Switzerland in the Nations League, desperate to see the Belgian get another win under his belt after a mixed start.

Much has been made of the new boss’ 3-4-2-1 system and whether it suits the pool of players available to him. Winger Ben Gannon-Doak has been shoehorned into a wing-back role at times, for example, while the back three was badly exposed against Switzerland.

However, Levein feels too much can be made of systems and has backed Pocognoli to find the right formula.

“He’s seen the boys in training, he’s done the research and looked to see what he thinks the best positions are," he insisted.

“He obviously puts them out in a system that he feels would be best suited to the players.

“Systems are funny because people can blame them, but you can get somebody who’s playing in a system who actually has a bad game. That isn’t the system that’s at fault.

“Sometimes one or two of the lads are just a wee bit off it and people are too quick to say the system’s not working when individual errors can lead to that. It’s quite difficult, especially for the manager when he’s getting to know the players as well.

“We have to trust the manager to pick the right system and the right players.”

During his own spell with the national team, Levein found it tough to strike up the same sort of relationships with players he enjoyed at club level, given the length of time he was able to spend with them.

This is another factor which suggests more patience may be required with the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager.

“At club level, you’re working with them every single day. You can get them in and have conversations on a regular basis.

“When you get these international players, it’s maybe for two weeks. They might have played two games the week before or played at the weekend, and you’ve got to give them some time to recover, so that’s time you’re not spending on the training ground.

“I think change takes time. Steve did a fantastic job, a really, really good job. The new manager is going to take time to work out what he thinks of the players and where he sees them playing.

“Getting a victory is quite important pretty soon. The players themselves need a wee boost and hopefully the manager can take a lot of confidence from that. Hopefully we can win at least one of these two games.”

"We've got a squad where, with us not having the game on (this) Saturday, we can look towards the Leicester game and use these two games (Exeter and Liverpool under 21s) to make sure everybody's in the perfect position come Leicester, which would be a huge task for us.

"So, yes, of course, it's another game that we want to win. Martin (Drury) will stress that enough.

"We do not like losing games and it's not on our radar at any moment, no matter who we're playing. So, we look to address that. We look to be positive.

"We look to get the performance, looking and feeling back how it has done (before Exeter) and then we look to build on that. We have a busy, busy schedule.

"Just because there's a game called off actually means it's busier, because we make sure we've got the time now and we've got the opportunity to prep and be perfectly positioned to go and play Leicester.

"I think we've seen that the whole squad's going to be so important. I think that's really key and I think Saturday and then obviously tomorrow night, with us not having a (league) game like until Leicester, it gives us an opportunity to kind of mould those games and it's about us being in the best position we can be for the whole squad, come Leicester."

#1995. How James McAtee became Nottingham Forest's tough-tackling 'quarterback': The heart-to-heart with Oliver Glasner, summer boot camp and an Adam Wharton blueprint

Published: 21:00 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 5 November 2026

Quarterback is not a word necessarily associated with somebody once dubbed the 'Salford Silva' but then James McAtee has changed immeasurably since leaving Manchester City 15 months ago.

That moniker was handed down when the diminutive midfielder was much younger, effortlessly gliding through City’s academy, excelling in tight spaces, never losing possession. Scoring heaps, too.

That is who Nottingham Forest thought they were purchasing for £30million in August 2025, a statement signing to play high up the pitch. And yet as last season unravelled, and the sackings piled up – four managers in all – McAtee mustered only two Premier League starts throughout the campaign.

He was given four minutes across almost four months at one stage and was an unused substitute in both encounters with City. That will change on Saturday, McAtee one of the first names on the Forest team sheet, owing much to one conversation with Oliver Glasner that changed the course of his career at the City Ground.

So to the quarterback. The most important position in a Glasner team. That was how the Austrian envisioned McAtee’s evolution, the path to regular matches, and within months he has become the heartbeat of a team that is deserving of significantly more points than the six they have amassed so far.

Those who oversaw McAtee's development at City are not shocked by the calm use of possession and incisive passes through the lines yet did not predict him flying into challenges and blocks, only two midfielders in the division having completed more tackles than his 14 so far. He has turned into a terrier.

James McAtee in his 'quarterback' role for Nottingham Forest, where he has become the heartbeat of the team

At Manchester City he was dubbed the 'Salford Silva' and was more effective higher up the pitch

This has been a product of a full summer’s work on a rented pitch in Stockport, close to the family home. Forest's sporting director George Syrianos had made it clear that McAtee needed to become more physically robust and, after a five-day holiday, he spent a regimented two-and-a-half hours a day training, including 60-minute weight sessions in the afternoons.

When he arrived back for pre-season, McAtee had put on just over 2.5kg of muscle and lost 1kg of fat. He turned up a new man and that served to rubber stamp Glasner’s idea of permanently moving him into the engine room.

The Forest boss spoke to the 24-year-old about how he had developed Adam Wharton at Crystal Palace into an England international and that the plan here would be exactly the same.

This month’s Nations League ties will come too soon for that yet there are those within the FA who are confirmed admirers of McAtee and expect him to earn future caps. That he skippered the Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament holds real weight inside St George’s Park.

Aesthetically, he is the picture of what the FA have wanted to create over the past decade: a nimble yet tough midfielder who guards the football with his life and wriggles out of trouble without fuss. And whose game understanding means he knows when to force the issue – McAtee has created the same number of chances as Rayan Cherki (18) this season.

The only central midfielders to have attempted more passes into the box than McAtee’s 60 are Bruno Fernandes, Granit Xhaka and Pascal Gross.

City will be some test on Saturday evening and there is plenty for him to prove, having worked under Enzo Maresca with the club’s Under 21s and a lingering feeling of what might have been at the Etihad Stadium.

As for England, they are blessed with real quality coming through in central midfield, with Alex Scott at Bournemouth leading the charge to unsettle the axis of Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice.

Scott could return from a thigh injury sustained during the last international break this weekend, a fitness problem that enraged his club.

McAtee skippered the England Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament

The 24-year-old bulked up over the summer and is now able to mix it in the Forest engine room

Beyond those three it is very much up for grabs. James Garner is a recent Thomas Tuchel favourite, largely owing to his work ethic, with Wharton overlooked for the World Cup.

The man picked ahead of all those, Manchester United’s Kobbie Mainoo, was not afforded a kick in the United States. McAtee’s defensive and offensive stats this season outstrip the others in that chasing pack. They all know that there is definitely a claim to stake for somebody.

It’s Rice, Anderson, Scott and another at this point. Whether McAtee can kick on beyond nine consecutive Premier League starts is up to him. Crucially, he is in control of his own destiny more than ever before.

At City, he patiently waited for chances that barely came. In his debut year at Forest, players considered safer bets jumped the queue as the club battled relegation. But under Glasner, he has been harnessed, given the assurances that one sub-par performance does not mean a spell on the bench. McAtee has always been somebody who needs love to flourish and has finally found some.

#1993. Huddersfield Town v Liverpool under-21s: Former Newcastle United keeper eyes career first - plus his two-fold Terriers role

The experienced Huddersfield Town goalkeeper, now 33, has represented ten clubs - in three different countries - and played for England up to under-18 level.

He has seen most things that football has to offer. But not a promotion. Not yet.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It is something that he dearly wants to put right at Huddersfield.

He'd obviously prefer a substantial playing role, but if that doesn't transpire, he will contribute in any way he can.

At League One level, Alnwick has played second fiddle to England under-21 custodian Matty Young so far this term.

The Hexham-born keeper has made two appearances in 2026-27, both in the EFL Trophy and a third will arrive against Liverpool under-21s tonight.

Town's qualification for the next stage of the Trophy is already assured and only a huge away win for Liverpool - which realistically shouldn't happen - will deny Town top spot in Northern Group H.

While the Trophy retains importance, the big priority remains league business.

Alnwick told The Yorkshire Post: "I've played in the Premier League, Championship, League One and in Scotland. I've dotted about a bit on loan at times. But I've never had a promotion, which is something that I want to achieve.

"I've been pushing because I know Matty's playing at the minute.

"The better he does and the better I push him, the more successful the club will be and the more successful I'll be. And obviously I want a promotion as well.

"I think that's not just the squad. I think that's the whole (club) staff.

"And when I say staff, I don't mean immediate staff. I mean all the guys around this place, the ladies who do the food and everything.

"It's about standards. This year I think they have gone up again.

"I think it's a collective thing. It's fans and everybody included who can really push the club to get a promotion."

Approaching his mid-30s, Alnwick - who joined Town on an 18-month deal from Cardiff in January - knows that his role is now two-fold. He has his own job to do in terms of doing everything he can to become No 1.

Equally, he understands that his seniority means that he is also a bit of a mentor for the club's younger keepers.

Especially fellow north-easterner Young, currently on international business with the Young Lions.

He continued: "I love it. For years and years, I've always tried to help the young goalkeepers.

"My aim is to play as many games as physically possible. That still hasn't left me. I still feel like a 21-year-old kid when you ask me if I want to play football.

"But I do also love helping people because I know goalkeeping is a tough world to be in.

"Especially with Matty, he's only 19 years old. I came through at Sunderland until I was 14 years old and then made the move to Newcastle.

"Actually his goalkeeping coach all the way through was also mine when I was a kid. So we've obviously had that connection straight away.

"He's a great lad. And I think he's done well this season. It's different from obviously coming from playing in League Two last season (at Salford) to a big club like this.

"But I think he's handled it really well and I'm helping him, but also trying to push him because it's healthy competition and I think that'll go a long way this season."

Alnwick counts himself fortunate to have learned from some big characters - and not just top keepers - during his grounding at St James' Park.

They include Steve Harper, who spent a loan spell at Huddersfield back in 1997-98.

"I couldn't have had any better and different goalkeepers at the time," he continued.

"When I was really young, Shea Given was coming towards the end, but Steve Harper was still there.

"And then the older ones above me were Tim Krul and Fraser Forster. All of them were really, really different goalkeepers.

"Then Rob Elliot came through as well, who had been and done the lower league stuff and then came to Newcastle.

"So I had a variety of different people to feed off different things because not every goalkeeper is going to be the same.

"I probably modelled myself more on Steve Harper because of the height and his style of play. But it's good to have all those sort of people around you. It's something that sticks with me."

Tonight's game with Liverpool (kick-off 7pm) is the precursor to a 10-day break for Town, who will return to competitive action at home to Leicester City on November 21 - their fourth consecutive match at the Accu Stadium in all competitions.

#1986. Meet Brighton's merry band of unlikely heroes: a midfielder taking tips from Lionel Messi, a twinkle-toed son of a ballerina and the £3m bargain now running the Premier League

Published: 02:00 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 02:00 EST, 6 November 2026

Noel Gallagher arrived at the Etihad Stadium at the weekend hoping to witness a repeat of his beloved Manchester City's FA Cup triumph, only to be sent packing to the soundtrack of the High Flying Seagulls.

That has been the story – no, not morning glory – of Brighton's season. Fabian Hurzeler's side sit third and are beginning to build a compelling case as the Premier League's most unexpected title challengers since Leicester City's remarkable triumph a decade ago.

Even Danny Murphy, rarely one for lavish praise, was impressed by what he saw after the City win.

'They are such a smart team and they are an absolute pleasure to watch with the ball,' he said on BBC's Match of the Day. 'They are brave. They find a way. They are tactically very good.

#1985. Worthing Women: Hero Woods is spot on

Worthing Women came from 3-0 down to take their League Cup tie at Camden Town to penalties, where goalkeeper Sian Woods made a pair of decisive saves in the shootout.

After experiencing a dry spell in front of goal at home to Sutton United seven days ago, Manager Jesus Cordon shuffled his pack to bring back the trio of Nicole Mackay, Kendall Varitek and the available again Skye Birkinshaw. Paige Baker-Carroll dropped down to the subs’ bench initially, alongside Hattie Rainey and Ludmila De Sousa.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Facing a side a division below them but with a 100% league record, the visitors took the game to their hosts during the early exchanges. Birkinshaw’s pace took her clear on the left, only for her cross to flash across the eighteen yard box with no one there to convert it.

Two minutes later, Ruby Melis conceded possession to Andrea Chan, with the former Islington Borough forward supplying Ice Kamara who curled wide of the target.

Clear-cut chances proved hard to come by for a while, until Kamara kept her cool to rob ‘keeper Woods and slot into an unguarded net, midway through the first-half.

Town, a team only beaten once in all competitions in 2026-27 - and that was at two-division higher Saltdean United in the FA Cup - rapidly gained confidence. Substitute Hannah Goffi combined with top scorer Maya Brueckner, to slip her teammate in for a shot which was confidently repelled by Brighton & Hove Albion loanee Woods. Chan unable to keep her effort down on the rebound.

Riding out the storm, a red Skye broke out when the Worthing winger fired in a deflected delivery that Mackay headed goalwards, netminder Maelie Rance kept out and a defender on the line cleared away from Varitek following up.

A brilliant diagonal pass by Neve McEvaddy then picked out Jess Richardson in the danger zone but Rance rebuffed at the expense of a corner.

Woods earned her corn once again, courtesy of a fine stop to prevent the partnership of ex-Lewes and Steyning midfielder Goffi and Brueckner from bearing fruit, shortly before the break.

Although the latter wouldn’t have to wait long to double the homesters advantage, as Woods uncharacteristically spilled the ball to present Brueckner with a simple opportunity to maintain her goal-a-game ratioThere was still time for an opening to fall to Annie Gracey in the ‘d’ but the Rebels attacker drove her attempt the wrong side of the post.

No sooner had the second period got underway than the visitors were staring down the barrel of a cup upset. An excellent through ball from the halfway line released replacement Amelia Shiner to calmly slot past the exposed Woods and seemingly put the game to bed.

Three short minutes later though, Rainey, part of a triple change at the interval along with De Sousa and Megan Gates, caused problems via a left wing corner that Sanaa Williams could only nod over the line amid her efforts to clear it.

Not long after the hour mark, a lack of bodies in the box cost the travelling Reds a go at pulling another goal back, thanks to Rance parrying Mackay’s long-ranger but with no red shirt close enough to capitalise.

Continuing to apply the pressure, within a matter of seconds Rainey sent in another troublesome flag-kick which resulted in Rance pulling off an incredible save to deny Captain Sophia Wickenden.

Then the woodwork came to Camden’s rescue, as De Sousa struck a piledriver that smacked against the crossbar from twenty-five yards.

Shortly after that, Worthing were also thanking the apparatus when Swede Minja Nilsson’s corner brushed the face of the same part of it.

A lowly four minutes were left on the clock at the moment Melis’ high ball into the box was glanced narrowly past the upright by Richardson.

Two more than remained when Brueckner got the better of Cristie Pritchard on the right and ultimately found Shiner who stung the palms of Woods, as the Towners looked to seal their passage through to the next round.

Most people thought it was all over, only for Makcay’s sighter from distance to create concern for the previously unflappable Rance. The Camden Cat caught out and unable to prevent the ball creeping over the line.

Not that the drama ended there, far from it in fact.

Teenage kicks by Rainey -  and not the Undertones - saw the youth team graduate receive a crossfield ball from Richardson, find space through the inside right channel and even less of it to squeeze a well-struck shot between Rance and her front stick. Queue pandemonium in the Rebels’ dugout amongst players and management alike!

So, penalties would decide the outcome of this second round matchup and, after successful conversions by Mackay, centre-half Ella Terry, Pritchard, Rainey and sub Baker-Carroll for the guests, Sian Woods stepped up to apparently send Worthing through to a third meeting of the season with Premier Division leaders Brentford, by way of frustrating Shiner.

Only for the Reds breakaway from the halfway line, to celebrate with their number one, to be stopped in their tracks by the eagle-eyed referee’s assistant. Meaning a retake for Woods prematurely moving off her line.

Undeterred however, an identical outcome caused the party to restart, thanks to the teenage stopper denying the same player twice in quick succession and, finally, sealing the Sussex side’s route through to round three.

If that wasn’t exciting enough for you, a visit from Aylesford to the Sussex Transport Community Stadium this coming Sunday sees Worthing take on a team below them in the Prem standings by just goal difference, as the Reds return to league action.

Leeds United star Dominic Calvert-Lewin has conceded he is in a “difficult position” behind Harry Kane in the England pecking order.

He has catapulted himself back into the England fold, but the presence of Bayern Munich’s Kane as the country’s chief marksman presents a significant challenge for the 29-year-old.

“His record speaks for itself,” said Calvert-Lewin ahead of England’s meeting with Croatia on Thursday (November 12). “He’s a fantastic player.

“He’s the captain of the country and he leads by example. And I think he’s deserving of his accolades at the moment. On a personal note, being a centre forward in competition for that place, it’s a difficult position to be in.

“So I think when I come away on England camps now, I think I have to be just as prepared as possible and ready for when my own personal opportunity comes, if and when needed.

Calvert-Lewin had gone nearly five years without an England appearance when he was ushered back into the ranks earlier this year.

“We’re both very different in the way we play. His mentality is very strong. We’re similar in that sense. We’re both very strong in how we want to play. His finishing quality, his overall quality and leadership is something I appreciate.

“Removing our own personal competition, striker watching another striker, he’s one of the best in the world and you cannot argue with that.”

England will host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing Spain in Madrid on Sunday (November 15).

#1977. Stephen Robinson was always wrong man for Aberdeen - what needs to change culturally and who next

Aberdeen have mercifully brought the axe down on Stephen Robinson’s ill-fated tenure as Pittodrie head coach.

The Northern Irishman arrived in the North East to what could at best be described as a mixed response from the Red Army. It was an appointment that smacked of desperation by Dave Cormack and the board, a ‘break glass in case of emergency’ scenario more than anything.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The decision wasn’t without merit. Aberdeen were in serious danger of relegation last season had they not done something and a head coach with Robinson’s extensive knowledge of the Scottish Premiership was a safe bet to navigate them away from that particular danger.

That alone was never going to be enough to endear him to the supporters who had been so vehemently against his arrival to begin with and, unfortunately, the former St Mirren boss did very little to win those boo boys over in the subsequent eight months. Unpopular signings who failed to hit the ground running and questionable comments to the press didn’t help but results were ultimately the deciding factor.

The biggest criticism levelled at the 51-year-old was that the Aberdeen job was simply too big for him. That has always been a bit of a vague statement but his tenure certainly didn’t do anything to prove it wasn’t the case.

It has also been said that chairman Dave Cormack doesn’t know what he’s doing when it comes to appointing head coaches. That certainly seems far closer to the truth.

The thing about all of the club’s post-Derek McInnes appointments is that most don’t share anything in common. It started with a young up and comer in Stephen Glass, followed by a flavour of the month appointment in Jim Goodwin and then giving the caretaker a shot after a string of good results with Barry Robson.

Then came the exciting foreigner with the bold tactical approach in Jimmy Thelin (let’s just pretend Neil Warnock didn’t happen shall we) and finally the safe hands of Robinson which proved to be anything but. Had Cormack been in a position to stick it out and hold on for Eirik Horneland - the apparent first choice prior to Robinson’s appointment - then you would have at least seen a pattern in the type of manager he had decided was what they wanted in the Pittodrie dugout.

Changing gaffers every year isn’t the problem, it’s the neck-snapping cultural shock in going from a Glass to a Goodwin to a Thelin to a Robinson that is the bigger issue. It almost doesn’t matter if the next manager and even the one after that doesn’t work out, what needs to be decided is the type of coach they want in the dugout and stick to that plan whoever it is.

So who and what will the Dons go for this time around? Will sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel pull an obscure name from the continent? Could recently appointed chief executive Adrian Bevington turn to his extensive contacts in English football?

In truth, they don’t need to look that far afield. In terms of who is out there in the Scottish top flight now, the talk of John McGlynn is completely warranted.

No, he’s not the glamorous name that is going to shift those mid-season ticket sales but it makes a lot of sense. He not only knows Scottish football but he knows the demands associated with a club of Aberdeen’s stature given his long association with Hearts where he also had a stint as their head coach.

Being in charge of Falkirk at their absolute lowest ebb in League One will have been a unique challenge as an almighty big fish in such a small pond and there will have been lessons from that he could take to Pittodrie. He’s got a great recent track record, a sensible head on his shoulders and doesn’t come with anything like the baggage that Robinson did surrounding his perceived negative tactics at previous jobs.

McGlynn’s Falkirk side, currently third in the league table, play good football. That’s not the huge sticking point that most people would have you believe is a non-negotiable for Aberdeen supporters but it does help.

Ask yourself though, if you were John McGlynn, would you trade your current job at Falkirk for the Aberdeen one? At 64-years-old he might not get many chances to manage a club of their stature again but, if I was him, I probably wouldn’t.

There’s another name that’s not being spoken about nearly as much that seems to tick a lot of boxes. St Johnstone boss Simo Valakari.

He’s got that combination of a strong understanding of the Scottish football landscape plus the overseas appeal to appease both sides of the supporters who are at odds over which they’d rather prioritise. He has developed a clear tactical identity for positive, front foot football which has earned him praise and seems to have cultivated an excellent dressing room atmosphere at McDiarmid Park.

Any time you ask a Saints fan or one of his players about the Finn their face seems to light up. Robinson had a likability issue as Aberdeen boss, that’s not something Valakari would struggle with.

No, he hasn’t got any experience with a club of Aberdeen’s size but what he can do is work miracles with a tiny budget and players who most probably wouldn’t have even considered Premiership standard before he got his hands on them.

If they’re looking to establish a brand for Aberdeen managers of the future then he’s the perfect patient zero. A positive character who wants to play positive football.

They needed an appointment last season to save them from the mess they had gotten into and this time around they have longer to steady the ship and push on. They have the luxury of some time to get the right man in, but not forever, so perhaps it’s best to ask the question now about what exactly they want their club to be and who is the right type of coach to enact that vision.

#1976. Romano: Milan remain obsessed with Inacio but Fonseca’s arrival could change things

It’s no secret that AC Milan will sign a defender in January, and one name is sitting firmly in the lead but he’s not alone.

Since the summer, Milan have been obsessed with the idea of signing Goncalo Inacio. His name was constant through the mercato and on deadline day, the Rossoneri tried to pounce on a last-minute deal. However, it was unsuccessful, understandably.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Within days of the mercato shutting, the Rossoneri were linked with another move in the January window and these suggestions have not gone away in the months since. Other names have been suggested, but again, Inacio remains the priority.

Speaking on his YouTube channel today, Fabrizio Romano offered an update on the club’s pursuit for Inacio ahead of the January mercato, via MilanNews.

“A defender will definitely arrive. He was supposed to arrive in the summer; he will arrive in January, so it’s no mystery. Milan also persistently sought him during the summer transfer window, an extra defender obviously in addition to Mario Gila, who was also an excellent investment by Milan, so the idea is to bring in at least another one.

“Milan reinstated Tomori a minute after the end of the summer transfer window out of necessity, but Milan’s idea is to take an extra defender. So a defender will definitely arrive.

“The name of Gonçalo Inácio must always be kept there because it is a name that has been in Milan’s mind since the first day of the summer transfer window; from when Ruben Amorim arrived until the last minute of the transfer window, he has always been in the thoughts anyway. There have been different attempts with different formulas.

“Milan had even considered, at a certain point at the end of August, a possible very expensive loan with an option to buy, so several solutions were considered that Sporting did not accept.

“Among other things, Sporting has changed its skin; Paolo Fonseca arrived on the bench, so we’ll see how much this will impact the dynamics of this operation. Clearly he’s not the only name, but Inacio is certainly a very welcome player; Milan has excellent relations with his agents, who are the same as Amorim.

“But I repeat, it doesn’t end here; there’s a list and Milan will make their choices.”

It’s a positive start that a defender will ‘definitely’ arrive; it’s just a case of whether they’re the right man now with Inacio not seeming like the definitive candidate.

#1974. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EST, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.

#1973. Martin Keown explains what he 'can’t quite fathom' after Leeds United's win over Tottenham Hotspur

Arsenal legend Martin Keown has conceded he “can’t quite fathom” a decision made by VAR during Leeds United’s 1-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur.

Daniel Farke’s side claimed three points at the expense of Spurs on Saturday (November 7), edging past the North London club with a late Noah Okafor winner.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It was not a game without controversy, as many felt Whites defender Jayden Bogle was fortunate not to see red for a challenge on Spurs winger Mathys Tel.

Keown is among those who felt Bogle was fortunate and has labelled the 26-year-old’s challenge as “reckless.”

He told talKSPORT: “It looks reckless. We’re just showing the clip, we’re not seeing it in real speed. I think he’s trying to somehow line him up to tackle him with his right foot. He plants his left and his left foot goes right down the Achilles of Tel.

“Actually, as he does it, he twists his ankle at the same time. It looks out of control. I’m pretty surprised, if we’re looking for consistency, I’m a little bit surprised he hasn’t gone for that. It does look poor.

“At least it should have been a yellow. It’s the studs, it’s the full six studs isn’t it? All the way down the back of the Achilles. I can’t quite fathom how VAR looks at that and doesn’t punish.”

Tottenham are complaining to Pro Ref about the decision and Keown’s surprise has been shared by former Premier League official Graham Barber.

He said: “I thought it was a very, very poor challenge, it was reckless at best but you could describe it as dangerous and endangering the safety of the opponent, and did it endanger the safety of the opponent? Well, the answer is probably yes, because he had to leave the field of play about five minutes later.”

#1972. Why Scottish football must take John McGlynn's managerial talent more seriously as passionate case put forward

Craig Levein believes Scottish football is guilty of overlooking one of its most impressive managerial talents, insisting John McGlynn has repeatedly demonstrated the qualities required to succeed at a bigger club – and even the Scotland national team.

The Falkirk manager continues to enhance his reputation after overseeing five consecutive victories, including Sunday’s 5-2 win over Hearts at Tynecastle, highlighting the consistency and quality of the work being carried out at the club. Yet, despite his dugout achievements at both Falkirk and Raith Rovers earning admiration, Levein is of the belief that McGlynn remains undervalued outside the clubs fortunate enough to have employed him.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Indeed, the former Scotland manager holds his old Tynecastle colleague in such high regard that he admits he would have handed him the national team reins. Having worked together in Gorgie, Levein insists McGlynn’s qualities were evident from the outset.

“I was promoting him for the Scotland job when it came around,” he confessed. “If you look at his record, it's pretty impressive. Raith Rovers and Falkirk, he’s pulling up trees at Falkirk just now. I just think he is undervalued, maybe not by the supporters that have had him as their manager but certainly in a wider sense in Scotland. He has done a brilliant job so far.

“When I went to Hearts at the tail end of my career, I was helping John do some training with the youngsters. Even then, you could tell immediately that he knows what he's talking about. John's eye for a player is pretty special. He's proved that over the years.”

It is that combination of football intelligence, vast experience, a calm temperament and attention to detail which makes Levein question why the meticulous 64-year-old boss has not attracted more interest from ambitious clubs operating at a higher level.

He suspects the changing trends in managerial appointments may play a part, with clubs influenced by perceptions surrounding age and reputation, rather than simply what a coach has achieved. Levein also believes there could be an element of snobbery when it comes to assessing managerial talent closer to home.

“If it was some foreign guy that had come in and done the same sort of job as him, I'm pretty sure he would have been promoted or moved to a higher level,” he stated. “I think he deserves to be working at a bigger club. I thought he had a chance to get the Scotland job. He's done all the work that he needs to do in my eyes to get an opportunity.”

There is little doubt that McGlynn's coaching methods have developed throughout his career. His time spent learning from Brendan Rodgers at Celtic allowed him to absorb new ideas and subsequently incorporate those principles into his own footballing philosophy.

Levein believes that demonstrated an ability to evolve without losing his own identity, explaining: “He went to Celtic, watched and learned everything on top of the knowledge he already had. The stuff he picked up from Brendan, he's implemented exceptionally well at Raith and at Falkirk. He's got integrity, knowledge, he delves into the minutiae when he's doing his team talks and makes sure everybody knows what's expected.”

Falkirk's recent performances have only strengthened the case. For Levein, there are no remaining questions about whether McGlynn can handle a greater challenge. The evidence is already there and becomes difficult to ignore.

“John's got better as he's grown older,” Levein added. “Quite a lot of times, guys who are coming in their 60s or 70s usually run out of energy. That's what catches up with guys getting into their later years. But he is relentless. Every box you want ticked, John would tick that box. I'm biased, I like the guy and what he does at football clubs. If I'm a chairman, all day long I'd be looking for somebody like him.

“He stays within the bandwidth of emotions. He doesn't get overly emotional during matches and he stays in this area, which I think is good for him and good for his players. You don't often see him throwing stuff about in the dugout or anything like that. He's a top manager who has improved enormously in the last five or six years.”
